item.title: How to Unclench
item.description:
I’ve spent the better part of a decade teaching nervous system regulation to thousands of people, and I’ve realized that most of what I teach distills down to one word: unclench.

~~

Picture the moment you step into a cold shower.

If you’re anything like me, you brace against the icy water.

But once you’re in, perhaps you gradually let go of this clenching.

And surprisingly, it’s not as bad as expected.

Possibly even enjoyable.

~~

This essay is about the life-changing impact of applying that same unclenching move to the rest of your life, in increasingly subtle ways. I'm sharing this essay with the LessWrong community to seek feedback, suggestions for a more rigorous research agenda and because I believe that being clenched a significant bottlenecks to our reasoning & decision making capacity.

We’ll explore how clenching keeps us stuck, practices for letting go, the freedom that lies on the other side and what progress looks like.

1. The Pain of Clenching

In 2001, Scott Boswell was seven years into his professional cricket career, enjoying one of his best seasons yet and gearing up for the biggest match of his life: a cup final at Lord’s.

"It was," he told a journalist, "going to be one of the best days of my life."

The night before, his coach told him, “Don’t fuck up.” This buried into his mind, and during his first over (for American readers, this is like pitching in baseball) he noticed his muscles start to clench. His fingers became so tense that he wasn’t able to release the ball.

The next over, he bowled wide. His muscles contracted tighter still, attempting to shut out humiliating jeers from the crowd. 

He bowled wide again, and again, and again eight more times… his mouth was dry, he felt like he couldn’t move. By the end, he was barely able to walk three meters to pick up a water bottle and asked his teammate to fetch it. It was one of the worst bowling performances ever recorded on live television. 

Boswell was sacked by his club days later, fell into a depression, turned to alcohol and spent the next ten years recovering.

This is an extreme case, and likely you’re not a professional athlete, but what has clenching (holding more tension in your body than necessary) cost you in your life?

I don’t mean just physical discomfort, but what opportunities have you squandered due to clenching?

I recall a student whose small intestine tightened like a ratchet as he defensively said words that ended an otherwise great relationship.[1]

And it’s not just the big moments — clenching affects us in subtle ways. If you’re anything like me, it looks like over-thinking a text reply, holding my breath whilst replying to email (so-called ‘screen apnea’), refreshing my Instagram feed, or overlooking creative third doors that would have unlocked serendipitous opportunities.


I received an email recently in which the self-aware sender described his default-clenched state in the following way:

"One of my biggest struggles is what I can only describe as the castration of my agency. The ultimate contrast is that I have an MBA, yet I’m driving a bus, which, as you likely know, is perfectly logical from the perspective of a stuck nervous system. My capacity is there, but my system won't let me access it."

I remember one particularly painful moment: walking into a subway station in London feeling like a zombie, as if there was a pane of glass between my life and my actual experience of life.

If you pay attention, in the moments when you are procrastinating on an important task, saying something your future self will regret or compulsively over-thinking, you are almost certainly sitting at the clenched end of this spectrum below.[2]

The more clenched you are, the fewer options you will perceive (see the slider animation below)


If you’re watching someone’s voice go high on stage while their posture stiffens, yep, that’s clenching nuking their charisma.[3]

In my experience it’s not only more difficult to feel emotions when I’m clenched, but extra difficult to receive compliments, accept help, express gratitude, celebrate wins or even spend money on themselves because it feels ‘indulgent’.

Try it for yourself as you’re reading this: deliberately clench your entire body like you're trying to vacuum-seal yourself from the inside. Now, try to feel an emotion: joy, pleasure, or anything at all.

You almost certainly won’t be able to. That’s because clenching drastically reduces the range of options and feelings available. It’s like paying an invisible tax on your experience: dulling aliveness and reducing perceived options.

Here's Oliver Burkeman, author of Four Thousand Weeks, describing his experience of the clench tax:

“Clenching seems to be my default response to uncertainty or overwhelm…to tighten up against them so as to hold them at bay – when in fact that leads only to paralysis and a sense of sterility.”

Four Years of Clenching

On the left is Evgeny Kobytev in 1941, the day he left for the front lines. On the right is the same man just four years later, aged thirty-four. Between the photographs: a wound, capture, two years in the Khorol pit (a camp where roughly 90,000 prisoners died), an escape, and a return to combat.

The museum that displays these photos puts it like this: ‘the first portrait looks at you, the second looks through you’.

During those four years his whole body went from feeling default safe (he worked as an artist) to default unsafe. The muscles in his face clenched to re-organize around the prediction that something bad was about to happen. Even long after the war ended, the clenches in his face and body remained firm.

2. Why Do We Clench?

The working definition I have for clenching is: unconsciously holding tension in a way that narrows your capacity to feel and respond.

And I mean this literally—clenching muscle tissue constricts blood flow, which prevents neurons from being updated.

Try this thought experiment: imagine an alien neuroscientist studying your behaviour on an ordinary Tuesday. He understands little about human culture, but he knows that mammals contract their muscles when preparing for danger.

His field report might read something like:

8:12 a.m. Repeated threats detected from a glowing rectangle.

10:43 a.m. Defensive contraction observed in proximity to another member of the species.

4:57 p.m. Muscular defenses activated anticipating critical feedback, apparently preparing to be punched by the future.

He might conclude that Earth is perpetually hostile. Alternatively, he might wonder why human physiology defends itself in the absence of an external threat.

The alien might reasonably ask: why do humans do this? What is their adaptive reason?

While there’s no established scientific explanation for why these patterns persist, I’ve come to view clenching as the biological system making a prediction – shrinking the uncertainty aperture on your experience to reduce overwhelming sensory input.[4]

Explain Unclenching Like I'm Five

The five-year-old version: imagine a protective character called ‘Big Clench’ who offers to protect the highly sensitive nervous system, aka ‘Little Feel’, from imminent danger.

Little Feel accepts the offer because it feels safer in the moment. But as the clenching accumulates, Little Feel’s life-force gets constricted: there’s less room for her to feel, play or follow impulses.

One common question I hear is: isn’t saying ‘unclenched’ just another word for ‘relaxed’? Nope. They’re different dimensions. You can be deeply relaxed (low-arousal, parasympathetic) and still highly clenched: depression and freeze live here. And a glass of pinot can unclench you without lowering your energy at all.

You can also be in a high-energy + unclenched state: this is where we typically experience creative flow, pleasure or expansive states like awe and wonder.

Theoretical neuroscience rabbit hole

A speculative model outlining how clenches get stuck and a proposed mechanism for how trauma is stored in the body.

The most compelling explanation I know of comes from theoretical neuroscientist Mike Johnson, whose vasocomputation model proposes that vascular clenching allows your nervous system to physically hold a prediction in place.[5]

In a recent paper, neuroscientist Ruben Laukkonen tracked brain dynamics during unclenching and showed that unclenching practice (the researchers called it ‘effortless awareness’) leads to what can be measured as ‘criticality’ on the level of the brain. Ruben describes this as:

“A system at criticality is exquisitely poised: neither rigid nor chaotic, neither stuck in what it was nor dissolving into noise. It is maximally sensitive, flexible, and synergistic. It efficiently processes what comes next”

One interpretation is that clenching opposes this flexible, sensitive, flow-like state. We have already made up our minds; our thinking has hardened; we no longer look for a third door.

When I was a kid at school, there was a teacher who was teased for ‘having a stick up her butt’. It wasn’t kind, but they were accurately observing that she had physical tension and also overly rigid beliefs.

Clenching swaps flexibility for short-term stability. By stiffening the body and narrowing available responses, it makes uncertainty easier to manage.

This offers a biological mechanism for the old idea that humans prefer the certainty of misery to the misery of uncertainty.

Some clenches last only a moment, like a flinch. Others become habitual: the same protective response comes even after the situation has changed.

According to Mike's theory, there are two different types of clenching:

  1. Short-term clenching: vascular smooth muscle constricts, reducing circulation to nearby neurons and their capacity to update.
  2. Long-Term 'Latches': When a clench is held for long enough, the smooth muscle tissue glues itself into a contracted state (latch-bridge mechanism), a state that could last for days, months, or even decades. Partial contraction becomes the new default.

These latches can cause numbness or greatly reduced sensation because the tissue receives less blood.

Latches are harder to release because muscle tissue has been chemically glued into a contracted state. Mike hypothesizes that this is how trauma is physically stored in the body.

It’s likely that addictive substances hook us precisely because they temporarily unclench the vascular system, and people come to depend on that relief.

~~

3. Clenching Protects Us From Feelings

Here’s a surprisingly deep question: why can't I just decide to unclench when I want to, in the same way that I can choose to unclench my fist?

Your body is making a reasonable adaptive choice.

For example, if, like me, you got angry at teachers as a kid, you were likely punished. Or if you cried on the playground, the other kids teased you.

Because we are social mammals, both experiences can lock in an adaptive clench. The next time the same emotions arise, we associate them with bad things, so push them back down to avoid the pain.

I would go as far as to say that most people have never fully experienced an emotion without clenching against it. If I could put one idea on a billboard for a billion people, it would be this:

Feeling a feeling isn’t what makes an experience unbearable. Our suffering comes from clenching against what we feel.

Here are five specific examples of common defensive patterns that arise due to clenching, along with the emotions being resisted, and the ‘brilliant logic’ that keeps the strategy of the clench in place.

This may sound abstract, so here’s a story from the first time I experienced unclenching into an intense emotion I had been avoiding.[6]

Back in 2017, my former fiancée, who was working as a junior doctor in the UK, had an anxiety attack at work, and proceeded to take her own life by overdosing on her SSRI medication.

The emotions were so intense that I unconsciously clenched against them. First came numbness, then guilt towards myself and anger at the medical system.

I felt ambushed by memories of our time together. I felt guilty even for laughing. I watched our shared dreams of the future self-combust into the abyss.

Six months later I found myself walking towards her memorial bench on a windy pebble beach. I could feel a flood of grief about to roll through.

I sank onto my hands and knees, my forehead touching the sand, and allowed myself to be taken by it. The tears gathered in a salty puddle.

Contrary to what I had feared, the grief didn’t crush me. Rather it felt like exquisite tenderness, opening into an overwhelming, primal sense of loving interconnectedness.

At first the experience confused me. I didn’t get it. I thought grief was supposed to be painful and bad, yet what I experienced was deep love and raw aliveness.[7]

Then I realised: it wasn’t the grief itself that hurt. It was my clenching against it that had been so brutally painful.

That moment on the beach changed how I related to my emotions. It wasn't about ‘staying strong’, but instead, letting my protective clenching armor fall away.

This took many forms, one of which was learning how to set aside my self-reliance—realising I needed friends and community, but that I had been terrible at asking for support.

Leonard Cohen’s lyrics became my daily reminder: ‘...there is a crack, a crack in everything. That's how the light gets in.’

4. Feeling Good is Our Default State

So if clenching leads to making decisions that you will likely regret later, then how do you become someone your future self will thank you for?

The mechanics of feeling really good are weird. You may believe that parts of your life need fixing because you don’t have enough money or the right partner. That story comes from cultural conditioning: an idea that we must somehow earn the right to feel good.

By now it’s a trope: a founder sells their company and falls into an existential crisis, or an Olympian wins gold and sinks into depression.

Fame and success simply amplify one’s internal state. Putting more points on your scoreboard of choice rarely creates lasting contentment. Or as Jim Carrey put it:

“I think everybody should get rich and famous and do everything they ever dreamed of so they can see that that’s not the answer.”

So how do we learn to feel good?

The default Western view is that feeling good must somehow be earned by adding things to your life. However, it is my direct experience that feeling good is our default state… when we remove the clenching.[8]

Letting go of tension raises the ceiling of happiness higher than most would imagine. The experience of deliberately unclenching feels like sliding into a deliciously-toasty Japanese onsen with an expansive view that you can’t help but go ‘ahhhhhhh’.

Dedicate a few hundred hours to the practice and your baseline of happiness becomes not a little higher but, according to serial unclenchers like Nick Cammarata, 30–50 times higher. And these unclenched states can become default traits.[9]

There’s another enormous benefit I’ve noticed: you stop feeling scarcity around feeling good. This is because if you genuinely believe in your ability to relax into a sense of fundamental wellbeing in less than half an hour, then you stop managing the world around you to make you feel a certain way.

II. The Unclenching Loop

If you only take away one thing from this essay, let it be this: unclenching is a trainable skill. But perhaps not in the way that you think.

Unclenching is like falling asleep—you cannot force yourself to do it, but you can create the conditions for it to arise.[10]

How do you create these conditions? By sending signals of safety to your nervous system.[11] The most effective way to do this that I have found is by running self-guided experiments, I call these loops.

I offer these practices with a caveat: unclenching is not yet a hard science. But we do need one.[12]

Unclenching is like stretching

Unclenching resembles stretching your hamstrings. Nothing in your anatomy prevents you from touching your toes, yet your body will not allow the range until it trusts you with it.

You can try this by exploring your breath, which is an excellent indicator as to how clenched you are moment to moment.

Pay close attention and you may notice a slight clenching on the inhale and softening on the exhale. After a few minutes, the breath often becomes quieter and the exhale easier to release.

1. Run Your First Loop

In AI, loops optimize a system. In research, loops run the scientific method. Here, the same logic applies to your mental and emotional life.

Try the 60-Second Unclenching Loop

Five simple steps to notice what unclenching feels like in your body.

Every loop has the same four steps: notice a clench, try a move (soften it, or tighten and release it), track what changes, then keep what worked and drop what didn’t. Here's a basic loop you can run in 60 seconds.

  1. Make a clenched fist with your hand → unclench/open it → notice how that feels.
  2. Hold your hands up on either side of you, so you can just about see them in your peripheral vision. Relax your gaze and then very gradually move them backwards until they fade from your view.
  3. Drop your lower jaw away from your upper jaw by about one-eighth of an inch so the teeth aren't touching.
  4. Notice a different part of your body that feels tight (maybe the face or belly) → see if you can relax in the same way.
  5. Hang out here, track how you feel and whether you spontaneously yawn or sigh, which indicates that your system is unclenching.

As you learn the basic moves, you can continue to look for increasingly subtle layers of clenching (eventually also including your perception and awareness) and run experiments when it doesn't come easily.

2. Self-Exploration Mode

The core principle can be framed as ‘cultivating a secure attachment with reality’. Or in plain English, helping your nervous system learn that it can be safe to stop clenching.

My favourite starting point is this:

‘Curious attention will dissolve your tension.’

Exploring what it is like to embody the perspectives of curiosity, playfulness or ease and noticing how your system responds is fertile territory for unclenching exploration.

And as we covered earlier, clenching can also protect us from feelings. If I were to distill the process down to a single question it would be: ‘If you couldn’t feel clenched right now, what emotion would you have to feel?’

I remember feeling clenched around a big decision I thought I needed to make in a few weeks. I kept going round in circles.

I stopped trying to ‘solve’ it and turned my attention to my body. What emotion was I resisting? I noticed a tight knot in my lower belly.

I put on some instrumental music and brought my awareness to the knot.

Almost immediately, my eyes welled up. My lower body began to shake a little and I allowed myself to soften, with my hands gently placed on my belly to invite ease.

I stayed with my breathing. It felt like my body was processing fear.

After a couple of minutes, I felt a constriction around my neck, almost like the experience of being strangled — and so reached for a pillow to make loud sounds into.

The intensity faded and a deeper layer of tenderness emerged. I wasn’t sure what it was connected to, though it felt linked to early childhood.

Sinking into this I felt a wave of relief and a deep sigh, which was a cue that my body was ready to drop into relaxation. I put on some relaxing music and lay there for a while, letting the experience integrate.

Afterwards, the looping thoughts were gone. My mind was clear and the ‘big decision’ now seemed like a non-issue.

Below is an example loop you can run for yourself:

As you clench less, you become more curious and as you become more curious, you clench less.

If you sense there may be an emotion present you can try listening to either the somatic surfing or the reparenting protocol guided sessions in the unclenching library. Or if you prefer a guided journey, I built an app for unclenching anxiety called Stateshift. You can try it on iPhone or Android.

Disclaimer: Some People Should Skip Self-Exploration Mode

Unclenching can bring intense emotions to the surface. If you have a history of trauma, or being in your body doesn’t feel safe, I strongly recommend starting with support from another person, ideally in person with a trained somatic practitioner. They can help you stay grounded if intense feelings arise and make sense of the experience afterwards. You can return to self-exploration when you feel more able to meet what comes up.

3. Unclenching in Human Connection

Playing the unclenching game both reveals clenches more quickly and makes them easier to soften.

When I argue with my wife, good intentions and questions of fault become irrelevant if I’m clenched: I know the conversation will end badly. Most arguments amount to two people saying, ‘I’m clenched, and it’s your fault.’

When I relax my defensive stance, however, the argument often resolves into deeper connection than we had before it began.

Outside active conflict, connection lets us borrow calm from another body. In one study, 110 people faced the threat of electric shock. Holding a stranger’s hand offered no clear benefit; holding a familiar person’s hand reduced distress and the brain’s threat response.[13] Co-regulation allows us to borrow nervous system safety from another.

At the most basic level, you can experience this when you hug or cuddle a partner, close friend or even a pet: you will notice yourself almost instantly unclench.

After a tough day, or when I have clenched myself into functional freeze, a few minutes of cuddling with my wife brings me back to myself. This gift is usually more effective than words.

~~

Where to Find Human Connection Loops

Ways to practise with another person, in person or online.

Across nine cohorts of Nervous System Mastery, we’ve found that students who report life-changing outcomes are almost always those who engage in our Relational Dojo practice. This practice can be summarized as unclenching while in connection with another.

There are several flavors of structured human connection loops.[14]

They all follow the same principle: practicing with another person makes unclenching easier and more sustainable.

You can also vividly imagine someone you care about, wish them well, picture them thriving, then intensify the image and the feelings it evokes.

I personally prefer practicing in person when possible. However, I've been pleasantly surprised by how powerful practice over Zoom can be.[15]

Why is human connection so powerful? In part, because it helps shame dissolve, and shame is often what keeps a clench in place.

Connection also reduces a core pitfall of self-exploration: it is surprisingly easy to bullshit yourself without external feedback, and eventually you reach limits of exploring solo.

If you’d like a structured way to practise this with others, this is part of what we do in Nervous System Mastery, my five-week cohort-based training. Learn more →

4. Laughter: An Ancient Unclenching Technology

A friend of mine says that "you can tell how much work someone has done on themselves by the depth of their laughter." Anyone can tell the difference between nervous or awkward laughter and a full, hearty belly laugh. The latter has less tension, less clenching, less defending.

Unsurprisingly, laughter involves cycles of clenching and releasing tension in the body. If you think of someone who is taking themselves too seriously, you will probably picture a curmudgeonly man in a tight suit with RCF (resting clench face).

By contrast, someone like the Dalai Lama seems moments from laughter. I can’t verify this, but I would bet that his belly ranks among the world’s most unclenched.

Also, consider stand-up comedy: hundreds of strangers paying one person to trigger involuntary spasms of the diaphragm. My suspicion is that the enormous comedy industry is, among other things, a cultural technology for collective unclenching.[16]

5. Leverage Temperature Change

Temperature change, often called contrast therapy, efficiently creates the conditions for unclenching.

In Finland, there are an estimated 2.4 million saunas for 3.28 million dwellings. That's one sauna for every 1.4 homes. (probably not unrelated that Finland ranked #1 in the World Happiness Report for the ninth consecutive year.)

The Finns have a word for the steam that rises when water hits the stones: löyly, from an ancient root meaning breath. An old proverb says to behave in the sauna as you would in church. By the third round, your system has a vivid experience of completing an activation cycle. The heat, much like humming, creates vasodilation (increased blood flow) + exertion followed by cooling and a parasympathetic rebound.

You can amplify the effect by actively unclenching during hot-cold rounds. After a cold round, sit, remain as still as possible, close your eyes, and unclench. The experience can become psychoactive and deeply enjoyable.[17]

III. Unclenching Traps

1. The Not Feeling Much Trap

Many people, particularly here in the Bay Area, navigate the world almost entirely through intellect.[18] Clenching has become the water they swim in.

They may not notice the clench because it is their only reference point, and the world pays them well for the abstract thinking that it enables. As Ken Robinson joked, the body becomes a way of getting their head to meetings.

If you’re in this category, start with the beliefs or rumination loops that create unease, then notice how they arise alongside tension in the body.

Begin with experiments that bring you into your senses and sharpen your sensitivity to anything that happens below the neck.

2. The Feeling Too Much Trap

Increased sensitivity is a superpower that requires an increased capacity to be with the intensity.

I think of the scene in Man of Steel, where young Clark Kent’s superhuman hearing switches on in the middle of class. It is so overwhelming that he hides in a janitor’s closet, and his mother talks him down through the door: ‘Focus on my voice. Make the world small.’ With time, he learns to be with the high stimulus and realises that it’s a gift.

On the positive side, this sensitivity may enhance your intuitive decision making and lower your tolerance for bullshit. It may even become harder to stay in a job you hate or a relationship that isn’t working because you feel the cost so acutely.[19]

The best skill that those on the more sensitive end of the spectrum can cultivate is grounding, which will build nervous system capacity over time. For this, practices like orienting, extended-exhale breathing and non-sleep deep rest (yoga nidra) are all extremely helpful.

Also on a practical note: being in a low-arousal environment (soft surfaces, warm lighting, plants or nature in view) can also make a substantial difference.

3. The Emotional Avoidance Trap

I mean, I get it. It's scary. It feels like there might be an endless torrent of tears and you don't know who you'll be on the other side.

But to paraphrase Anaïs Nin, your life will expand or contract in proportion to your courage. And just twenty seconds of courage can go a long way.

The sequencing is also important, it’s almost always preferable to start with increasing your nervous system capacity with gratitude, joy or pleasure. And then from this resourced place you can begin to turn your attention to the difficult thing.[20]

Something I notice is that most people are comfortable expressing either their sadness or anger, but rarely both. And often many people I work with default to sadness (rather than anger) and need to re-learn how to welcome their anger specifically.

A Cheat Sheet for Feeling Anger

How to prepare, feel anger safely, and avoid the common failure modes.

Anger Is Essential

If you always clench against anger, you will find it difficult to say no, set boundaries or advocate for your needs. Essentially, people won’t trust you, you’ll fall into people pleasing tendencies and likely accumulate resentment over time.

Signs of Clenched Anger

Possible signs include resentment of others, an active inner critic (anger turned inwards), a lack of aliveness or a sense of dullness (as if you’re living behind a pane of glass), or difficulty saying no to others’ requests.

How to Prepare

Set aside 15-25 minutes, find a private space (unless you have a friend or loved one who is open to holding space and witnessing). Ground yourself, drop into your body, and if you can, connect to the care/presence that the anger is protecting — and specifically where you feel the anger in your body.

Prioritise safety and remove any sharp objects, hard surfaces, etc. Optional but helpful: play an activating track or music (here’s a track I use)

How to Feel Anger

Once you’re connected to the sensation, there are three approaches to try:

  1. Setting a boundary or saying ‘no’, which can be done by pushing as hard as you can against a wall with sound/growling etc.
  2. The ‘it’s not fair/tantrum’ which can be done lying on your back (on a mattress) and pounding the bed/pillows with your fists.
  3. Using a tennis racquet or striking with your forearms onto a pillow whilst making loud sound or saying ‘fuck you’ (surprisingly effective but be careful with your vocal cords)

Watch out for shame/judgement arising as you’re doing this. You can try the phrase ‘I am loved in my anger’ or ‘I love my anger’ (whatever feels most supportive to you). Typically, especially in the beginning, either it'll feel fake or the anger will come out kinked. That’s great. You can keep acting angry until it feels real.

You will likely oscillate between being in your head/story and connecting to the somatic sensations. This is also totally fine + normal. Also, lower-pitched sounds or growls (from lower down in the belly) tend to be just as effective but do not cause vocal cord impact in the way that higher-pitched screams can. With practice, the heartfelt sensations of anger will be easier to access, as will the deep sense of care that it comes from.

You will know when something has shifted, as there will typically be either relief, or another emotion will surface (potentially heartbreak, or helplessness) that the anger is guarding against.

Failure Modes to Avoid

  1. Being aggressive towards others. If you’re blaming someone else, you’re not taking responsibility but projecting how you feel onto someone else.
  2. Disembodied raging/screaming which may feel cathartic but likely won’t create the associations of safety you’re looking for. Rather let the movement arise from the core of your body (often the belly).
  3. Overriding yourself ~ the goal is to re-pattern your system so that anger is safe to express, and that you are loved in your anger.

Core takeaway: the more grounded and connected to yourself (or to the care that your anger is protecting) you can feel before, during and after the practice, the more naturally anger may flow over time.

I've spent the last few years exploring emotional territory that I previously wouldn’t have touched with a ten-foot bargepole. Anger, shame, helplessness, terror… and time and time again these deeply contracted places open up into profoundly meaningful experiences where I feel more connected, more integrated, and more fully myself.

Above all, I’d suggest taking it slowly, being gentle, and trusting that you will be brave enough to meet the moment when you’re ready.

4. The Stoicism Trap

This is one I see often (and it was me for a long time). Aspiring Stoics or long-term meditators, perhaps practicing with vipassana or Stoic self-control training, have figured out a way to witness emotions at arm’s length. This can often lead to peace, but also a state of feeling less aliveness and being triggered by seemingly small things.

I call this the Stoicism trap. It’s seductive because it feels like an improvement on being trapped in the existential washing machine. Here’s the key difference: mindfully witnessing an emotion is very different to moving towards it with care and compassion.

Imagine how you would treat your son or daughter if they came to you with a big emotion. You wouldn’t (I hope) just passively observe them from a distance. You’d give them a big hug. Well it’s no different with your own internal feelings.

5. The Over-Efforting Trap

As my friend Michael Ashcroft likes to say, 'The Appropriate Amount of Effort Is Zero': the act of ‘efforting’ is itself a form of clenching. Trying harder to unclench is therefore a common pitfall.

There is a chasm-wide distinction between setting a strong intention and over-efforting. At a high level, action can happen naturally, without trying.

Examine your frame of reference. If you approach the practice thinking, ‘I need this to work’ or ‘What’s wrong with me? Why can’t I do this?’, that frame is itself a form of clenching.

When the body feels safe and relaxed, the clench opens at its own pace. You can create the conditions, but you cannot force the timing. So if the unclenching practice isn’t helping, you might try asking yourself ‘how might I create the conditions for the clench to release effortlessly’

Applying the achievement-based orientation toward improving ourselves is part of a wider frame that itself unclenches with time.[21]

If you’re clenched about being clenched (i.e. frustrated at the pain and then frustrated at your frustration), then turn your attention to the resistance of your resistance.

Or as the poet David Whyte says: ‘start close in, don't take the second step or the third, start with the first thing close in, the step you don't want to take.’

The principle here is that you cannot force yourself to let go, but you can let go of forcing yourself. It just requires humility and the vulnerability inherent in letting go of control.

Just as you wouldn't judge an oak sapling for not being a 300-foot-tall tree, we are all at our own particular vantage points, growing at different paces and on different trajectories.

6. The Midwit Grinding Trap

Yes, clenching hard, white-knuckling your way through life, especially in the beginning of a career, can get a lot done.

But this is a “midwit” approach to productivity, and it often ends in burnout years later. I’ve worked with dozens of formerly clenched founders and executives. Enjoyment is a far cleaner fuel source to run on, and will take you to far higher levels of excellence in your craft.

Changing the source of your motivation usually involves a transition period. You may feel as though you have lost your edge; I liken this to the process of ‘deschooling’.

Deschooling is the decompression period children undergo after leaving mainstream education. They may do little for weeks or months before their curiosity returns. Then they become super-learners, devouring books and starting projects for fun rather than on command.

Unclenching can be a powerful performance enhancer.[22] Take Alysa Liu, whose father poured $1m+ into her career at age 13. The extreme control and regimen helped to mold a teenage prodigy, but came at the cost of her agency, curiosity, pleasure, or any life beyond skating. So at 16 she got tired of being under the clenched grip of her father and quit for two years to travel, study, play, and learn.

Eventually, her curiosity for skating returned. She agreed to come back only on her own terms: no strict control of her food, and a say in the music and choreography. A few years later, in February 2026, she won Olympic gold in Milan at age twenty, joyfully crushing her competition and treating the ice as her canvas.

7. The Unclench Everything Trap

Unclenching has an optimal pace, yet there is often a temptation to force clenches open before they’re ready. I fall into this trap all the time myself.

In fact, the urge to unclench everything at once itself comes from a tightly clenched place (yes, it’s clenches all the way down).

Patience and titration work wonders: move gradually, leaving time to integrate and recover.

Sure you can force some clenches open with psychedelics or holotropic breathwork, and this might be extraordinarily beneficial because it gives you a glimpse as to what being unclenched can feel like. But without safety, the clench will return once ordinary consciousness resumes.[23]

Unclenching Loops Are Non-Linear

The idea of progressing 1% every day is a myth. Unclenching will not progress in a linear fashion. It more resembles scientific exploration: many routes end in failure before one produces an apparent breakthrough.

You might also go through a phase when you feel extra clenched. This is common and it's generally a result of increased sensitivity.

The environments and people you like to be around may shift too. This can be challenging, especially if it means relationships coming to an end.

This process may feel destabilizing at times. This is normal and also a signal to be gentle with yourself and if possible work in person with a somatic practitioner to support with integration.[24]

Then one day, you will eventually wake up and notice that vibrancy has leaked back into life, along with a sense of background wellbeing that no-one can take from you. Eventually, you may even look forward to the moment that you feel clenched. You’re excited to get to know it, explore it and creatively love the living daylights out of it, because you’ve seen that it inevitably melts into more joy and freedom.

IV. What Does Progress Look Like?

Level 1: Default Mode

Default Mode Stage → running on default mode where reactivity runs the show. You don't realise you're in a game. Others perceive you as emotionally volatile, distant or shut down.

Internal narrative → "why is the world so unfair? What did I do to deserve this? It's the fault of [external person or situation]"

Relationships → attract partners that mirror reactive tendencies. Reactive tendencies clench against intimacy, meaning that lasting fulfilling relationships are challenging.

Strategies → addictive coping strategies provide temporary relief from clench-induced suffering, but don’t last. There will likely be many crutches, either in the form of substances or behaviors (porn, sugary food etc.)

Core Challenge → there's insufficient curiosity about what's happening internally. The pain hasn't yet been enough to provoke real change. Unfortunately, often it takes a burnout, breakup, personal loss or a health crisis to create sufficient humility.

How to Progress → empowering practices and discipline help at this stage to increase a sense of 'self-authorship' as well as sincere inquiry along the lines of asking 'how might I be complicit in creating the conditions I say I don't want'.

Level 2: Unclenching Novice

Early Agency Stage → you start to realise that you can influence your internal state. The first crack of awareness appears. Still reactive, but now there's a witness. This creates more confidence and amplifies curiosity.

Internal narrative → "wait... maybe I'm contributing to the clenching. Maybe I can do something about it. Perhaps I don't have to believe everything I think."

Others perceive you as → still reactive... but there are moments of self-awareness that weren't there before. People notice you sometimes catch yourself mid-clench.

Relationships → you begin taking responsibility for your side of conflict, even if you still sometimes blame first. After an argument, you notice: "Aha… my reaction was disproportionate to what actually happened. Was I clenched?" As a result, repair conversations and moments of intimacy are more accessible.

Strategies → you recognise the tension in your body as you're doom-scrolling. The half-life of reactivity is still long, but you can see it happening. The more you notice, the more the auto-clench reflex starts to break down.

Core Challenge → awareness without change. You can see the pattern but can't reliably interrupt it (which feels frustrating and adds to the clenching)

How to Progress → move from noticing to actively running experiments (see above). Try one body-based practice and track what happens. The shift to Level 3 happens when curiosity overtakes frustration.

Level 3: Unclenching Practitioner

Active Experimentation Stage → Now you're actively running unclenching loops for yourself. You track which practices actually work for you (maybe cold showers help, but meditation before coffee makes you anxious).

Internal narrative → "Wow, this is fascinating, look at all the various ways I've been reacting and defending against my emotions. I wonder what else there is to discover."

Others perceive you as → More grounded, but also sometimes more sensitive to environments or humans that lead to dysregulation. At times, this can feel disorienting and you might seem like you're "going through something" to others.

Relationships → You can catch clenching at 2/10 instead of 9/10. During a heated conversation, you notice and say to yourself: "Oh, I'm getting defensive." The Reactivity half-life is dropping from days/weeks to hours. You might need to pause in conversation more often, but when you come back, you're more present.

Strategies → Coping mechanisms become conscious choices rather than automatic defaults. You have a growing toolkit and know which practices work for specific situations.

Core Challenge → It sometimes feels like you're going backwards. More sensitivity means more feeling, and less guarding means more vulnerability. The increased awareness can be overwhelming before integration and capacity catch up.

How to Progress → begin to explore and embrace underlying feelings that are being clenched against. Grounding practices help but eventually you need to make the move towards welcoming and feeling the underlying emotions.

Level 4: Unclenching Adept

Integration Stage → the unclenching skills that once required conscious effort are becoming automatic. Your default state is easeful and the underlying emotions are generally welcomed. You notice increased sensory clarity and unexpected ripples of joy in ordinary moments and your half-life of reactivity has shrunk to minutes.

Internal narrative → “I feel like good things just seem to be happening, but I don’t know if I can take the credit”

Others perceive you as → calm yet warm, present but not intense. People feel safe around you and remark that you're "grounding to be around"

Relationships → you can hold space for others' activation without getting pulled into it. Conflicts become opportunities for deeper connection and aliveness rather than threats to be avoided.

Strategies → unclenching that once required conscious effort now happens automatically. Someone might deliver harsh feedback but you’re able to receive it with appreciation.

Core Challenge → subtle identification with being "the unclenched one" — a new (superior) identity can form around your progress that itself becomes surface area for reactivity. You may also avoid situations that threaten your hard-won equilibrium.

How to Progress → let go of the identity of being ‘unclenched’. The shift to Level 5 involves loosening your identification and reducing the surface area of self so there's less to defend.

Level 5: Unclenching Master

Master Stage → emotions arise, are felt fully moment to moment and pass through without leaving residue, such that there’s almost no lag between experience and integration. You have opened into secure attachment with reality.

Internal narrative → "Everything is workable. I can’t believe that I get to have this experience. What a privilege."

Others perceive you as → people can't quite articulate what's different, but they feel the aura and wish to be around you.

Relationships → deep intimacy with everyone and everything. You can be fully seen without flinching because there’s no longer anything to defend or clench against or story about what it means.

Strategies → there's less surface area of identification to be caught in. Perhaps you notice excitement when something challenging arises, because you know that the other side holds even more freedom.

Core Challenge → the work at this stage is staying open and continuing to deepen in devotion to the people, work and place around you and it feels like a constant joy.

How to Progress → There is no final destination and progress is inevitable. In the moments when subtle clenching still arises it is understood that the suffering itself is a dense bundle of love.

Running unclenching loops creates a high agency virtuous cycle, although it takes some agency to run one in the first place (as opposed to blaming external circumstances).

The clench narrows the vessels supplying nearby tissue. Less blood can get through, so the cells receive less oxygen and fuel and clear waste less effectively. That leaves them with less spare energy for the metabolic machinery that restores relaxation.

Mainstream mental health practitioners are rightly starting to pay attention to the role of metabolic health, but very few (if any) factor in the role that clenching plays.

4. Origins + Possible Mechanisms

i. A Brief Intellectual History of Unclenching

Wind the clock back to 500 BCE and Siddhartha Gautama (aka the Buddha) figured out unclenching. In fact, he called it the Second Noble Truth: that clenching (tanhā in his language) is the root of suffering (dukkha).

Thousands of years later, in the nineteenth century, psychotherapists pioneered what we now loosely call ‘somatic work’.

Wilhelm Reich argued that chronic psychological defences show up as ‘character armour’: rigid personality patterns. He used breathwork, direct manipulation, and emotional release to dissolve it.

Soon after, his student Alexander Lowen mapped chronic muscular holding patterns into the ‘five character structures’: five clenching styles the body learns, often early in life, to defend against feeling unsafe or unwelcome.

Then, unfortunately, the field of psychotherapy took a turn away from the body and moved more into the realm of 'talk therapy', which can be a helpful first step but, in my experience, rarely addresses the root cause of suffering.[39] It's common to hear of someone going to therapy for a decade without any significant breakthroughs or shifts in their life.

ii. How the Body Might Keep the Score

Towards a Biological Mechanism for How Trauma is Stored in the Body

Neuroscientists have recently pushed back against the idea, popularized by Bessel van der Kolk, that the body keeps the score (one article was subtly titled: 'The Body Keeps the Score Is Bullshit').

Neuroscientists such as Lisa Feldman Barrett argue that everything, including trauma, is in our heads. Barrett argues that actually “the brain keeps the score”, essentially dismissing the idea that trauma somehow lives in the body.

Many of these critiques are valid: as of today, there is no established bodily mechanism for storing trauma.

Here's a quote from Professor Andrew Huberman:

“The operational definition of trauma is that some fear took place and somehow gets embedded or activated in our nervous system and shows up at times when it’s maladaptive.”

Note that he says somehow it gets embedded or activated in our nervous system.

To see why this gap matters, go back to the early 1800s.

In that era, physicians knew that diseases spread, but they didn’t understand how or why. They saw fevers sweep through towns. They watched infections spread from patient to patient. But they couldn’t see what was causing them.

So their best theories were guesses: maybe it was bad air, moral weakness or an imbalance in the body’s humors. Some observers, like the physician John Snow in the early 1850s, suspected invisible agents, but no one had actually seen them.

And crucially, microscopes and laboratory methods were not yet good enough to establish that specific bacteria caused particular diseases. Then, in the late nineteenth century, there was a shift that changed the course of humanity.

Improvements in microscopy, staining and culturing made microbes visible and testable. In the 1870s and 1880s, Robert Koch developed methods for linking specific bacteria to particular diseases. Once these pathogens could be identified, researchers had a precise target for prevention and, eventually, treatment.

Once the invisible became visible, the entire field transformed. Right now, in mid-2026, I wonder if we might be on the cusp of a similar breakthrough in the science of trauma.

Mike Johnson is a soft-spoken savant. A renegade philosopher and neuroscientist operating outside of academia, he is best known for his theories on 'neural annealing', the 'symmetry of valence' and, more recently, what is in my view his most ambitious theory: 'vasocomputation'.

If those terms are unfamiliar, don’t worry. What matters here is how they relate to the unclenching hypothesis.

Mike’s theory is that vascular tension acts as a special type of memory, which allows the brain and nervous system to store predictions about the world (known as priors).

Everyone was taught in school that the vascular system is just “plumbing for blood”: tubes that transport nutrients and waste.

Mike’s theory suggests this misses the vast majority of what the system does: the vascular system adaptively shifts tension to help neurons compute. In other words, our vascular system is like a giant biological computer, where a single sustained thought is a pattern of vascular tension.

For the trauma story, the key property of these vascular clenches is the ‘latch-bridge mechanism’.

In simple terms, a latch creates a semi-permanent clench, which deprives neurons of blood and further prevents updates. In experience, this becomes a fundamental prediction through which we see the world (Scott Alexander calls this a trapped prior; Sasha Chapin calls it 'Gnar').

A recent study published in Nature appears to support the idea that psychedelics, and in particular serotonin, have powerful vasoactive effects, lending support to the idea that at least some of the benefits of psychedelic-assisted therapy are related to their ability to support unclenching.

The Latch Pod

One of Mike's ideas that I'm obsessed with is his dream of building a latch pod. This futuristic device would be able to scan your entire body (much like the Midjourney ultrasound) to create a latch map as a diagnostic for how clenched the person is.

The pod would then use tFUS or another mechanism to help the outermost layer of latches soften and open.

At one level, opening these latches might resemble processing and integrating trauma, as may happen in psychedelic-assisted therapy. At another, depending on a person’s capacity, releasing deeper latches might loosen the priors associated with the self and create something resembling classical Buddhist enlightenment.

Explore in 3D ↗


Let’s play out how this future could unfold and what it might mean:

  • There is a Latch Research Institute and we’re able to use fMRI + contrast or elastography to successfully identify latched areas.
  • From there, we could A/B test somatic modalities to determine which actually help.
  • We’re able to see which chronic and untreatable diseases are downstream of latch formation.
  • We’re able to test the conditions under which latches naturally open up and remain open (a lot of it seems to be related to a sense of loving presence that the client/practitioner has). My guess is that Hakomi, NARM and certain forms of breathwork are extremely promising here, but we would be able to confirm this with data.

5. Speculation Corner

i. Somatic Luck Theory

I have a working theory that unclenching makes you measurably luckier. Here, ‘luck’ combines three factors that unclenching may influence:

  1. Increased Tolerance for Uncertainty: Less contraction creates a sense of inherent safety in the world, which expands your sense of the ‘adjacent possible’, increasing your capacity to sit with ambiguity and giving novel connections more time to emerge → thus reducing the odds of picking a low-risk default path.
  2. Attract High-Integrity Collaborators: Others track the reduced bracing and receptive nervous system state, which signals trust and connection (via micro-expressions, low facial tension and HRV coherence). This leads to more generous assumptions about others' motives, which in turn lowers defensiveness and boosts opportunities.
  1. Repeatedly Uncanny Decision-Making: Individuals holding less tension will naturally gravitate towards choices that aren’t driven by subconscious desires rooted in emotional avoidance. Instead, they tend towards actions with a higher payoff due to state-dependent intuition.

In short, less tension may clear perception, improve decisions, and make life appear to bend luck in your favour.

ii. The Four Clenched Horsemen

There are four so-called 'Horsemen' of major degenerative diseases – the four biggest killers on the planet – and all of them are downstream of inflammation in the body.

“Although there may never be such a single path, mounting evidence suggests a common underlying cause of major degenerative diseases. The four horsemen of the medical apocalypse — coronary artery disease, diabetes, cancer, and Alzheimer's — may be riding the same steed: inflammation.” — Harvard Health Publishing

What's fascinating is that there are clear theoretical mechanisms for how clenching and latches would create the conditions for inflammation, and therefore perhaps be an upstream root cause for the leading causes of death among humans.

Research has found associations between adverse childhood experiences (i.e. latch-generating trauma) and a higher risk of certain cancers later in life. For example, a study of 1.2 million people found higher breast and cervical cancer incidence among young women exposed to high childhood adversity, but no clear association with overall cancer incidence in men.

This is highly speculative. But needless to say if there were even a one-percent chance that vascular latches help sow the seeds of four leading causes of death — cancer, diabetes, heart disease and Alzheimer’s – the hypothesis would deserve rigorous study, which to my knowledge no-one is yet doing.

It may also be the case that GLP-1s like Ozempic have effects on the smooth muscle tissue (could this be related to the reported loss of sex-drive and addictive tendencies)

iii. The Potential Role of Bioelectricity

Dr. Michael Levin might be the most interesting scientist of our generation. Among many things his lab has shown that bioelectricity is used to send signals within organisms and help them maintain coherence. And recently it has been demonstrated that all living cells emit small amounts of light (biophotons). His peer-reviewed paper on platonic space picked up 1.3M views on X (it’s rare for scientific papers to go viral).

Levin’s research suggests something wild: that agency, the capacity to sense, decide, and act, isn’t exclusive to humans, or even to brains. Cells and tissues exhibit a kind of decentralized intelligence.

“Agents can combine into networks, scaling their tiny, local goals into more grandiose ones belonging to a larger, unified self.” — Dr. Michael Levin

This is astonishing. There may quite literally be something it is like to be a lung cell.

Levin’s team has also shown that cancer cells are often electrically disconnected from the body’s bioelectric field, visible via fluorescent voltage-sensitive dyes.

In this light, cancer isn’t just uncontrolled growth: it’s a kind of cellular dissociation. A forgetting of the larger coherence. A soloist who’s lost the key.

What makes this story even more compelling is that your body is awash in bioelectric gradients.

These voltage patterns are foundational to healing, tissue regeneration, and even embryonic development (possibly also disrupted by high EMF environments). Your cells aren’t only responding to chemical cues: they’re listening to bioelectric signals.

And Levin is attempting to decode this language: to read the score that cells use to know who they are, where they belong, and what song they should be singing.

What we call “love” (or “safety”) may literally be a bioelectric signal. The heart produces the body’s strongest rhythmic bioelectromagnetic signal. At the body surface, its electrical signal is typically tens of times larger than the brain’s. When coherent, it radiates in rhythmic waves through tissue and space.

I speculate that the practice of loving kindness (what Buddhists call "metta") might be able to up-regulate coherence in living organisms, which in turn creates the conditions for the latches to open and for the cells to reconnect with the broader bioelectric field.

Could loving presence send a signal that helps latched tissue loosen and restore healthier patterns?

I don’t know. But again these questions seem worth exploring and advances in AI may soon (if not already) make them scientifically testable.

item.title: You don't need a union to go on strike
item.description:
I read Dear God, Please Do Not Resign In Protest and wanted to point out that leftists have a mature and relatively reliable set of strategies to address the problem of how to get a lot of people to stop working in protest at the same time.

Then I did a search of LW to see if someone else brought unions up already, read What if AI safety labs unionized?, and flinched at the repeated citation of reasons why a union isn't the correct legal structure and the absurdly complicated legal structure that was being suggested instead. So no, what you want right now isn't an official, bureaucratic union. In fact, that would probably slow things down too much.

But I've done enough work with union people to know that you don't need to go through the traditional channels. You don't need to have a majority vote supervised by the NLRB; pre-majority unionism is a legitimate strategy. You don't need to be striking for a contract; you can just be striking for an individual concession. A strike does not have to be leaving the workplace and making a picket line; work slowdowns or still doing work and just giving it away for free can be effective too (the latter is technically illegal but can be scarily effective). You don't need to have an official union structure backing you; wildcat strikes happen all the time. You don't even have to want to start a union at all.

All you really need for a strike is something unacceptable happening, and people deciding to walk out together because of it. Everything else is fluff.

If you're reading this and need help going from "disgruntled" to "collective action", the Emergency Workplace Organizing Committee gives one-on-one mentorship on how to start doing union-adjacent work, up to and including providing and roleplaying social scripts (you'd be surprised how necessary that often ends up being). At the moment, they respond within 24 hours to most inquiries. Usually they focus on building up union power privately in the back first, but if you make it clear this is a flashpoint and you need to seize the moment, they'll work with that too.

(I'm mostly hoping this somehow gets sent to a privately disgruntled frontier lab employee, but it would also be cool to expand other people's minds on the way there.)

item.title: The Game is Set for a Targeted Memetic Attack on the AI Safety Community
item.description:
While this is relevant to my work at MIRI, I have not checked these ideas with anyone else on the team and am posting this on my personal LW account. These views are my own[1]. And to be honest, I am writing this mostly to remind myself of my weakness.

---

I expect one (or many) adversarial memetic attacks aiming to trip you up, perhaps consisting of fake leaks relating to dangerous stuff happening in the labs. Specifically, worrying incidents that may fit snugly within your worldview, leaking from multiple sources including news outlet/s, but not confirmed/confirmable by a primary source. Think rumors about exfiltrated weights, AIs attempting to create viruses, agent swarms hacking into and gathering information from nuclear infrastructure, etc.

An easy way to remove status from a movement is to trip it up: make it fall for a misinformation trap in public, then use that slip-up to discredit the movement for all time. The game is set for a memetic attack like this. There's a well-resourced group waiting for your screw-up.

And then you may remember much that will help you. 

In public and in private, if you feel surprised or confused, notice your confusion. These feelings are signs that your world model doesn't match reality.

Real incidents make you want to act fast. You feel the need to contact journalists, tweet about the incident, and start telling your friends: a memetic attack will feel the same. If you let them trip you, you burn credibility. Set a 5-minute timer and write out your thoughts before acting. Ask yourself:

  1. Where is this information from?
  2. Do I trust the source?
  3. Can I verify any of this information myself? [2]
  4. If I must act now, is there a way that I can take action while remaining visibly skeptical of the claim and its source?

item.title: Two Axes of Alignment: A Framework for Robust Superintelligence Alignment
item.description:
1. Summary

I classify alignment research along two axes: forward-chaining vs. back-chaining reasoning and extrapolative vs. invariant justification of the safety property in question. I argue that extrapolation is insufficient to justify confidence that the safety property will hold while crossing into the superintelligence capability level, whereas an invariant justification is necessary. I also claim that while forward-chaining from current models may give us useful safety properties and even local invariants, back-chaining from superintelligence aims to find the jointly sufficient set of safety properties for alignment. Hence, I argue that robust superintelligence alignment (denoted RoSA instead of RSA, to avoid confusion with RSA encryption) requires approaches that back-chain from superintelligence and establish invariant safety properties. Some of the ideas here draw on existing alignment thinking. My aim is to synthesize these ideas into a useful framework for considering alignment approaches, specify the requirements for robust alignment, and give potential objections.

2. Two Axes of Alignment Research

Axis 1: Research Direction (starting point of reasoning)

Forward Chaining (forwards from current AI): Start with current systems and develop methods that make them safer as capabilities increase.

Backchaining (backwards from superintelligence): Determine properties necessary to align a superintelligent AI, and then work backwards to develop methods or architectures for alignment.

Axis 2: Basis of Reasoning

Extrapolation: Observe a method that preserves a safety property for a model at a capability level, then infer this holds as capabilities scale. Methods that are part invariant still classify under extrapolation, as the justification still must rely on a fundamental extrapolation.

Invariant: A safety property has a formal or structural argument establishing its invariance across capability transitions.

The Four Quadrants of Alignment Research

Axis 1/Axis 2

Extrapolation

Invariant

Forward Chaining

RLHF/RLAIF; behavioral evaluations and red teaming; model-organism experiments; empirical AI control; pragmatic mech interp

Ambitious mech interp

Backchaining

Empirical tests of debate and IDA; weak-to-strong generalization

[RoSA lies in this quadrant] Agent foundations; alignment focused learning theory; theoretical analyses of debate and amplification

Note: The quadrants are idealized categories. In practice, there may be overlap for alignment approaches.

3. Why Extrapolation is Insufficient for RoSA - Persistence

Let an alignment target specify how the model is to act aligned. I will remain agnostic as to the correct alignment target. For this framework a model will be considered robustly aligned if it satisfies some specified alignment target at some reliability, independent of domain.

Our confidence in alignment can be justified via an extrapolative or invariant basis. Empirical success forms an extrapolative basis. A formal or structural proof forms an invariant basis.

Thus, I can state my argument as follows:

Premise 1: Superintelligence will operate outside of the capability regimes in which our alignment methods can be empirically tested.

Premise 2: Empirical success within one regime does not establish that a safety property will hold outside of it, especially as novel failure modes may arise in new regimes.

Therefore: Empirical success of a safety property within a pre-superintelligent regime does not guarantee that property will hold in a superintelligent regime.

A superintelligence is robustly aligned if we can provide an invariant formal guarantee that the alignment target is satisfied in all viable environments. Any claims of alignment that rely on extrapolation of empirical evidence for justification are non-robust.

Thus, we see there is an issue of persistence. We cannot guarantee a safety property will persist outside of regimes it was shown to have empirical success in.

4. Why Forward Chaining is Insufficient for RoSA - Completeness

Following from establishing the need for invariants to determine RoSA, we can then similarly address the second axis of forward-chaining versus back-chaining and have a quadrant that specifies approaches to determine RoSA.

Forward chaining from current models may be instrumental to RoSA (refer to section 5) even if FC does not itself constitute a robust solution to superintelligence alignment.

The problem is one of completeness. Forward chaining from current models may allow us to discover local invariants that hold across regimes. However, because FC is bottlenecked by models we currently have, we may overlook potential failure modes where invariants are needed when in the superintelligence regime. Solving every failure mode of today with an invariant does not guarantee we have the required set of invariants for superintelligence. Essentially, FC may discover some/all of the required invariants, but it can’t establish the set is complete.

The required set of invariants can only come from back-chaining as this would require inspecting the potential failure modes of the regime that we expect to deploy our model in. If researchers are able to find all the failure modes, we could construct the jointly sufficient set of invariants to guarantee RoSA.

Thus, I can state my argument as follows:

Premise 1: RoSA requires a set of safety properties jointly sufficient to satisfy the alignment target in the superintelligence regime.

Premise 2: Forward chaining does not guarantee that the failure modes observed will establish the properties jointly sufficient to satisfy the alignment target in the superintelligence regime.

Premise 3: Establishing completeness requires backchaining from the alignment target in the superintelligence regime to determine safety properties jointly sufficient to satisfy the target.

Therefore: RoSA must include backchaining from superintelligence to determine the complete, jointly sufficient set of invariants.

A superintelligence is robustly aligned if we can provide an invariant formal guarantee that the jointly sufficient set of invariants satisfies the alignment target in all viable environments. Any claims of alignment that rely on extrapolation of empirical evidence to justify or derive a set of invariants from forward chaining are non-robust.

5. What Forward Chaining Is Good For

The ways forward chaining is valuable:

  1. Bootstrapping robust alignment: Forward chaining may be used to develop an automated alignment model strong enough to provide backchained safety properties and invariant justification, which (hopefully) we can then independently verify.
  2. Reducing risks from current and near-future models: Evals, red teaming, control, and preference fine-tuning can mitigate failure modes in current models.
  3. Generating empirical information about alignment failures: Finding failure modes and seeing how alignment properties fail as capabilities increase.
  4. Providing testbeds for theoretical ideas: These tests may lead to invariant or structural justifications down the line.
  5. Enabling a safer transition: These methods may buy time for RoSA.

Thus, I do not claim that forward chaining has no value, as FC may contribute substantially to reaching RoSA. My claim is instead that FC alone cannot establish RoSA.

6. Conclusions

The central claim of this post is that we need backchaining for completeness and invariant justification for persistence to establish RoSA. Forward chaining is clearly useful in the buildup of this idealized alignment solution, particularly in the case of automated alignment, but FC itself will not establish RoSA.

Thus, FC and extrapolation may help us reach RoSA, but backchaining and invariant justification are required to establish RoSA.

7. Objections

Extrapolation is better than I claim.

Perhaps empirical evidence across sufficiently diverse systems can provide extremely high confidence. An alignment method might succeed across sufficiently diverse regimes to justify high confidence, even without an explicit invariant. Simply stating “extrapolation is not proof” may be insufficient justification.

Robust superintelligence alignment may be impossible.

Establishing the alignment of a superintelligent model with the required confidence may be impossible. Backchaining may be fundamentally impossible if we cannot find a useful framework to consider a superintelligent model.

item.title: The Horse
item.description:
You have a horse.

You do not like the horse. The horse does not like you.

At the moment, you are completely dependent on the horse. The terrain is impossible to traverse on foot. There is no way to travel without a horse. You wish that would change, but when you tell other people, they laugh and call it impossible. A few get angry.

You must spend hours each day feeding, cleaning, and taking care of the horse. You must spend even more time working to earn enough money to pay for the horse's needs. The horse is often unsatisfied with your offerings. No matter how expensive and time consuming your efforts, the horse will desire something more unique, exciting, or comforting.

The horse also requires a third of your day to sit and do nothing. During this time, you cannot do anything or go anywhere.

If you do not comply with the horse's desires, it will make your life miserable.

People tell you that, as the horse's rider, you have complete control over the horse. Somebody must have forgotten to tell the horse this. If the horse is hungry or thirsty, it will draw your attention towards its needs at the expense of your own. If the horse is afraid of something, it will run away with you on its back. If the horse is hurt, it will whinny and curl up and refuse to move, even if the injury itself is not severe. If the horse sees a sufficiently attractive horse of the opposite sex, it will drive you towards it, regardless of the embarrassment it causes for you and the other rider. There is nothing you can do about any of this.

Some people find great joy in pampering their horse, giving it the sweetest and most varied meals or grooming and garnishing it with the most beautiful decorations. Others take pride in the strength and ability of their horses, winning competitions, playing games, and achieving great feats. You're happy for these people, and respect the hard work they invest into their horse. You wish they wouldn't judge you for refusing to do the same. You wonder what these people will find joy in once their horses are old, once they are no longer healthy or strong or beautiful.

Oh, yeah. Once the horse dies, you will be completely cut off from the world and everyone in it. Most people believe you ascend to another world, better if you were virtuous and much, much worse if you weren't. Some people think that you cease to exist at all. Regardless of your thoughts on the matter, you would rather choose the time to exit this world, rather than staking it upon the horse, which is notoriously fragile and inevitably deteriorates beyond repair.

When you express this to other people, they shake their heads and tell you that you need to accept the passing of your horse. You don't see why; technology is becoming more advanced each day, with people attaching increasing sophisticated carts and plows to their horses, attaining increasing sophisticated knowledge regarding the relationship between horse and rider, and even creating funny little automatons which could roll without a horse at all. You once proposed that someone create one large such automaton for you to ride around in, horse-free, and people sighed and called it a wonderful dream. Many people who are smarter, more resourceful, and more influential than you have tried and failed to build it. You wish you could help.

Many act as if you were opposed to the concept of leaving the world at all, citing the justice of the next world, the meaning that the scramble to do everything and meet everyone you desire before your horse decays gives life, and the sheer impracticability of a cramped world from which no one could escape. This hasn't changed your opinion much; you aren't opposed to death, you'd just like a choice.

After your anti-horse positions became known to your companions, they attempted various lines of reasoning to return your common sense. One told you that the horse was made in the image of God, which doesn't sound right, because God doesn't need a physical form to get around and, without a rider, the horse is just a dumb beast, no different from any other. Another told you that she couldn't imagine life without a horse. You can. A third told you to be grateful that the horse is healthy and able, and that there are plenty of people who want nothing more than to have a sighted, able horse with four working legs and without dysfunctional organs or chronic pain. You feel sorry for those people. You wish that there was a way to remove them from their failing horses and give them something functional, or even superpowered, to ride. When you said this, your friend glared and called you unfeeling, although you expect many of the people he claimed to sympathize with wish the same.

You did not choose, nor can you change, the horse that you are given. Regardless, most people will judge you by the appearance of your horse rather than the content of your character. Some will judge you by the horse's color, sex, and breed. The more enlightened will insist these traits are meaningless, and judge your horse's face, stature, and mane, even if they deny it. If your horse is sufficiently unattractive, your career, relationships, and self-confidence will suffer, irrespective of your ability, virtue, or achievements.

You wish your time, your reputation, and your very life were not defined by the horse, a mere beast whose only purpose is to carry you and perish. You dream of a world in which nobody rides a horse unless they want to, in which people think and experience in ways that horse riders couldn't imagine, in which nobody would be forced to leave the world before they are ready. Unfortunately, you fear your companions are right and such a world is impossible. You want to prove them wrong, but you have no idea where to start. In the meantime, you will go to work, you will dream of a better world, and you will take care of your horse.
